summary: Top hypothesis H4 (medium, 0.60): an inbound login-traffic surge (~4x) from outside the platform exceeded auth-service's provisioned capacity ceiling, saturating its fixed 64-worker pool and its maxReplicas=8 autoscaler cap, filling the accept queue and producing 503s on POST /v1/auth/login with p99 stepping ~40x to ~3.75-4.0s at 06:54Z. The mechanism and demand-side driver are verified on telemetry: request_rate rose from ~394 to ~1642 req/s starting in the 06:48-06:51Z interval, rate_limited_per_min exploded ~400x, CPU saturated at 96-98%, worker queues reached ~94k, the autoscaler was blocked at maxReplicas 8, and the only 503 signature in logs is "accept queue full ... (POST /v1/auth/login)". The reporter's bcrypt-regression hypothesis (H2, rejected) is excluded: zero auth-service deployments in the window or prior week, no config/flag change near onset, and no bcrypt/timeout/OOM log signature; the shared-redis-cache hypothesis (H3, rejected) is excluded by flat cache CPU/connections/evictions and latency-flat co-tenants. Residual uncertainty is confined to the origin sub-hop (external flood vs original-caller retry) and login-endpoint confinement, both of which the platform's metric layer cannot measure; neither changes the mechanism or the immediate mitigation.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Inbound login traffic surge (external flood / credential-stuffing) overwhelms auth-service capacity ceiling
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An inbound request surge driven from outside the platform (~4x, appearing simultaneously at api-gateway and auth-service) exceeded auth-service's provisioned capacity. With a fixed 64-worker pool and maxReplicas 8, the service hit its ceiling: CPU saturated (~97%), worker queues grew to ~94k, the accept queue filled, and POST /v1/auth/login was rejected with 503s while p99 stepped ~40x to ~3.75-4.0s. Rate limiting exploded ~400x. No code, config or dependency change near onset; memory and restarts normal.

causal_chain.claim: An external flood starts: api-gateway request_rate and auth-service request_rate rise in the SAME 120s bucket (gateway 1227.99->1500.82, auth 386.14->452.43 at 06:50Z), with comparable ~4-4.7x rise factors, so the increase is not amplified downstream of the gateway.
Auth-service inbound rate climbs from ~394 req/s baseline to 671.71 (06:51Z), 1154.93 (06:54Z), peaking 1641.69 avg / 1813.74 max (06:57Z), holding ~1400-1550 req/s.
Load is far beyond provisioned capacity and actively rejected: rate_limited_per_min jumps from ~1.5-2.3/min to 607.72 (06:54Z) and ~885-916/min sustained (~400x).
Auth-service CPU climbs from ~36-40% to saturation ~96-98% from 06:54Z onward; CPU saturation precedes/coincides with latency and error onset.
Worker pool saturates (active=64/64, queue=39035, queues reaching ~94k) from 06:54:53Z; autoscaler desired 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8 and cannot scale.
Accept queue full -> 503 rejections, whose only error signature is 'request rejected: accept queue full ... (POST /v1/auth/login)' (372 occurrences); 5xx rises from ~0.1-0.32% to ~11.7-14.4%.
p99 steps ~40x from ~82-97 ms to ~3.75-4.0s in the same 06:54Z bucket; api-gateway shows the same 06:54Z step (error_rate to ~9%, p99 to ~3.87s), carrying the excess load.
Alternatives excluded: memory stays 48-57%, restarts 0, no deployment within 64 min of onset, no config/flag change near onset.

assumptions: The surge originates OUTSIDE the platform (external flood / credential stuffing) rather than from upstream callers retrying. Evidence strongly disfavors gateway-side retry amplification (timing and magnitude match; gateway always forwards MORE volume than auth-service receives), but the same magnitude match would also be produced by the original external caller retrying directly against the gateway, which cannot be separated from a single-pass flood without source-of-traffic (IP/UA) or per-route data.
The surge is concentrated on POST /v1/auth/login; this rests on the 503 signature being exclusively that endpoint, since no per-endpoint request_rate dimension exists.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Auth-service internal capacity/queue saturation at its provisioned ceiling (mechanism-only, demand driver unidentified)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: Auth-service saturated its fixed resources — 64-worker pool and an 8-replica autoscaler ceiling — so the accept queue filled and POST /v1/auth/login returned 503s with ~4s queueing latency. This hypothesis deliberately strips out the demand-side origin: it asserts only the verified mechanism (fixed pool + replica cap + queue growth + accept-queue rejection) and is agnostic as to whether the driver was an external flood, an upstream caller retrying 503s, or some other load source.

causal_chain.claim: Demand on auth-service exceeds provisioned capacity (driver not identified here).
Auth-service CPU climbs to ~96-98% saturation from 06:54Z.
Worker pool 64/64, queue ~39k-94k; autoscaler pinned at maxReplicas 8.

assumptions: None beyond the mechanism: this is retained only as the fallback mechanism should H4's external-origin hop be disproven in favour of an internal or caller-driven overload.

ranked_hypotheses.title: External kyc-provider stall blocks auth login workers
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The unobservable external kyc-provider (has_telemetry=false) began stalling calls from auth-service's login path, holding workers until the pool and accept queue saturated, producing 503s and ~4s p99. No evidence shows the login path invokes kyc-provider synchronously, there is no timeout or upstream-error signature in auth logs, and the decisive node is unobservable by construction.

causal_chain.claim: kyc-provider is an external dependency on auth-service's path with no telemetry.
kyc-provider latency/errors increase at ~06:54Z.
Auth workers block on slow external calls until pool 64/64.
Worker starvation -> accept queue full -> 503s and ~4s p99.

assumptions: a stall would hold workers long enough to fill a 64-slot pool at observed throughput

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation after portfolio-service v4.4.0 holds auth-service workers
ranked_hypotheses.statement: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803, 05:50Z) loaded the shared redis-cache that auth-service also depends on, stalling auth cache calls and tying up workers until the 64/64 pool saturated. Cache CPU, connections and evictions are flat through onset, all three redis-cache co-tenants and the deploying service itself are latency-flat, and timing (64 min gap) fails.

causal_chain.claim: portfolio-service v4.4.0 deployed and exercises redis-cache heavily.
redis-cache is the sole shared component coupling portfolio-service and auth-service.
Shared cache slows, stalling auth cache calls.
Stalled cache calls occupy auth workers until pool 64/64.
Worker starvation -> accept queue full -> 503s and ~4s p99.

ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Direct cache telemetry (F26 CPU flat ~22%, F28 connections flat ~309, F29 evictions flat ~3/min) plus all three redis-cache co-tenants latency-flat at 06:54Z (F30, F31, F35) and the deploying service itself healthy (F30) rule out the shared-cache mechanism. Timing fails: the 05:50Z deploy is 64 min before onset with no change within the 06:48-06:54Z adjacency (F14, F17, F15).

ranked_hypotheses.title: Reporter's hypothesis: auth-service bcrypt cost/code regression reintroduced
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An auth-service release raised the bcrypt cost factor as in HIST-101, making each login CPU-bound ~4s and saturating CPU/workers, producing 503s. No auth-service deployment exists in the window or the prior week, no config/flag change exists near onset, no bcrypt signature appears in logs, and the precedent was deployment-triggered with no counterpart here.

causal_chain.claim: An auth-service release introduces a higher bcrypt cost factor.
CPU rises from hashing work.
Worker pool saturates and accept queue fills, yielding 503s.

assumptions: A bcrypt-cost change could occur without any recorded deployment (feature flag or unsearched mechanism).
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Zero auth-service deployments in window or prior week (F2, F14, F1); no config/flag change near onset (F15, F16); no bcrypt/timeout/OOM signature in logs — only 'accept queue full' 503s (F11); precedent HIST-101 was deployment-triggered (F6, F18); symptom is a step change at 06:54Z unrelated to any auth change (F8) and coincides with a ~3-4x inbound rate surge (F20, F24) that the bcrypt mechanism does not explain.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency was flat at ~82-97 ms through 06:48Z, then jumped ~40x to ~3.75s in the 06:54Z bucket (3752.4 ms avg / 4012.81 ms max) and stayed elevated ~3.7-4.0s through end of window.
auth-service error_rate rose from ~0.1-0.32% through 06:48Z to 11.72% in the 06:54Z bucket and settled at ~13.7-14.4% thereafter, in the same onset bucket as the latency jump.

auth-service CPU climbed from ~36-40% (through 06:42Z) to 56.79 avg / 96.96 max in the 06:48Z bucket and saturated at ~96-98% from 06:54Z onward; CPU saturation precedes/coincides with latency and error onset.

The only error signature in auth-service logs is 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' (372 occurrences, first_seen 06:55:42Z); there is no bcrypt, timeout, connection-refused, or OOM signature.

auth-service WARN logs show capacity exhaustion from 06:54:53Z: 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' and 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (first_seen 06:57:15Z); queues reached ~94k.

auth-service inbound request_rate was flat at ~382-413 req/s through 06:48Z (avg 394.82 at 06:30Z), then rose to 671.71 (06:51Z), 1154.93 (06:54Z), peaking 1641.69 avg / 1813.74 max (06:57Z) and holding ~1400-1550 req/s; the surge onset (06:48-06:51Z) precedes/coincides with the 06:54Z latency/error onset.

rate_limited_per_min was ~1.5-2.3/min through 06:51Z, then exploded to 607.72 (06:54Z) and ~885-916/min sustained to 07:30Z (min 0.8, max 949.79), confirming load far beyond capacity was being actively rejected.
auth-service memory_pct stayed normal at ~48-57% across 06:30-07:30Z including onset (52.23 avg at 06:54Z; max never above 57.07), so memory exhaustion is not present.
auth-service restarts ('restarts' metric, cumulative) were 0 across the entire 06:30-07:30Z window (all buckets avg 0.0, max 0.0), excluding pod crash/restart loops.

Zero auth-service deployments occurred in the incident window or the prior week; the only deployment across all services in the window was portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) at 05:50:00Z ('CSV export endpoint'), and re-querying 05:00-07:30Z returns exactly that one deployment, 64 minutes before onset.

No config or flag change occurred near the 06:54Z onset (query for all services in 05:00-07:30Z returns count 0); the only config change in the early window is cfg-2801, auth-service log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40Z by config-bot ('Reduce log volume'), 194 min before onset and unrelated to auth-path code or bcrypt cost.

The cited precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14, bcrypt cost 10->14 raised in release v6.4.0, resolved by rollback) was a deployment-triggered event, and no auth-service release exists near this onset, so the precedent's trigger mechanism has no counterpart here.

redis-cache (the only shared component on auth-service's path) stayed healthy through onset: CPU flat (mean 22.09%, max 25.59%), connected_clients flat (mean 309.15, 305.63 at 06:55Z), evictions_per_min flat (mean 2.96, 3.06 at 06:55Z), and no latency/error metric exists for it.

All three redis-cache co-tenants and the deploying service itself were latency-flat through the 06:54Z onset: portfolio-service p99 ~180ms, pricing-engine ~60ms, market-data-service ~40ms, with no deviation at onset.

api-gateway error_rate jumped from ~0.13-0.24% (through 06:51Z) to 6.23% in the 06:54Z bucket (plateauing ~8.85-9.53%) and latency_p99_ms jumped from ~204-217ms to 3869.46ms (max 4024.51) in the same 06:54Z bucket, matching auth-service's onset boundary.

api-gateway and auth-service request_rate first rise in the SAME 120s bucket (06:50Z): gateway 1227.99 (06:48Z) -> 1500.82 (06:50Z), auth-service 386.14 -> 452.43; gateway climbs to ~4.3x and auth-service to ~4.5-4.7x, comparable multiplicative factors.

Absolute request volume at auth-service never exceeds the volume api-gateway forwarded in any aligned bucket (06:50Z 1500.82 vs 452.43; 06:54Z 3294.15 vs 1094.83; 06:58Z 4790.49 vs 1749.75), which is inconsistent with retry/duplicate amplification at the gateway and consistent with genuine inbound load.

No per-endpoint or per-route metric dimension exists on either auth-service or api-gateway (queries for request_rate_by_endpoint and requests_by_route returned not_found; each exposes only 7 service-level series), so the login-confinement reading rests on the 503 signature, not a per-endpoint measurement.
The only endpoint-level evidence anywhere is in the logs: the 503 rejections are 100% POST /v1/auth/login; no other endpoint appears in any rejection signature.

redis-cache is the sole shared component on auth-service's path (also serving portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service), so the combination of healthy co-tenants and an auth-path-only gateway error/latency jump isolates the fault to auth-service rather than shared infrastructure.

assumptions: The ~4x surge originates OUTSIDE the platform (external flood / credential-stuffing) rather than from upstream callers retrying, or from the original external client retrying directly against the gateway. Same-bucket onset, matching rise factors, and gateway volume always exceeding auth-service volume disfavor gateway-side retry amplification, but a single-pass flood cannot be separated from client-side retries without source-of-traffic (IP/UA) data.

The surge is concentrated on POST /v1/auth/login. This rests on the 503 rejection signature being exclusively that endpoint, because no per-endpoint request_rate dimension exists; a service-wide ~4x rise on all endpoints would be indistinguishable in available metrics.
The surge onset lies inside the 06:48-06:51Z interval; the true onset is bounded by the 6-minute bucket grid rather than pinned to an exact second.

No undiscovered change mechanism (schema migration, feature-flag flip outside the config system, cron/job change) altered auth-service behavior near onset; change search covered deployments and config only.

The failure mechanism is demand-driven capacity saturation rather than an auth-internal slowdown; the alternatives (bcrypt code regression, shared-cache degradation) are contradicted on the available evidence, but kyc-provider (has_telemetry=false) and a DB-side contributor restricted to auth-service traffic cannot be observed.

timeline.event: Only early-window config change: cfg-2801 flips auth-service log.level INFO->WARN by config-bot ('Reduce log volume'); 194 min before onset, unrelated to auth-path code or bcrypt cost. It also suppresses INFO per-route request logs.

Only deployment across all services in the window: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803), 'CSV export endpoint', status live, not rolled back. Portfolio-service shares redis-cache with auth-service; 64 min before onset.
Last clean baseline bucket: auth-service p99 flat ~82-97ms, error_rate ~0.1-0.32%, request_rate ~386 req/s; CPU climbs in this bucket to avg 56.79 / max 96.96.

Surge begins inside the 06:48-06:56 interval: api-gateway and auth-service request_rate rise in the SAME 120s bucket (gateway 1227.99 -> 1500.82; auth-service 386.14 -> 452.43). No change event in this adjacency.
auth-service request_rate reaches 671.71 req/s (rise begins between 06:48Z and 06:51Z buckets), rate_limited_per_min still near baseline (1.46/min).

Onset bucket: auth-service p99 steps ~40x to ~3.75s, error_rate rises to 11.72%, CPU saturates ~96-98%, request_rate 1154.93, rate_limited_per_min explodes to 607.72. api-gateway shows the same 06:54Z boundary (error_rate 6.23%, p99 3869.46ms).
auth-service WARN: 'worker pool saturated (active=64/64, queue=39035)' — first capacity-exhaustion log.
First 503 rejection logged: 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)'.
auth-service WARN: 'autoscaler: desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' — autoscaling pinned at its ceiling; request_rate peaks 1641.69 avg / 1813.74 max.
Incident INC-008 reported by on-call SRE as SEV-2: login latency ~4s and 503s, suspected bcrypt regression per HIST-101.
Single 'clock drift ... resyncing with NTP' WARN in auth-service logs (isolated, not a recurring signature).

Conditions sustained: auth-service p99 ~3.7-4.0s, error_rate ~13.7-14.4%, CPU ~96-98%, request_rate ~1400-1550 req/s, rate_limited ~885-916/min, worker queues to ~94k; gateway request_rate peaks 5247.87. All three redis-cache co-tenants remain latency-flat; no restarts; memory normal.
Last observed 503 'accept queue full' rejection; incident still active at latest data (08:59Z).

recommended_actions.action: Relieve the auth-service capacity ceiling by raising the autoscaler maxReplicas above 8 (observed desired=14 exceeding maxReplicas=8) and/or expanding the fixed 64-worker pool, so the queue (~39k-94k) and accept-queue-full 503s can drain.
recommended_actions.rationale: The immediate bottleneck is verified: worker pool saturated at 64/64 with queue to ~94k and the autoscaler unable to exceed maxReplicas 8; p99 ~4s and 13-14% error rate persist until headroom exists.

recommended_actions.action: Apply/enable aggressive rate limiting and blocking on the login path at the edge (api-gateway / auth-service rate-limit rules) for POST /v1/auth/login, targeting the offending source; the platform's rate limiter is already rejecting ~900/min, so tighten and extend the throttle at the edge where the surge first appears.
recommended_actions.rationale: The surge arrives at the edge and is rejected downstream: gateway and auth-service request_rate rise in the same 06:50Z bucket and rate_limited_per_min jumped ~400x, so throttling at the ingress point reduces load without waiting for capacity changes.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back or revert portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) as a mitigation for this incident.
recommended_actions.rationale: The deploying service is latency-flat (~180ms p99) through onset and shares redis-cache with auth-service only via a demonstrably healthy cache (CPU, connections, evictions flat); rolling it back would not address the verified cause.

recommended_actions.action: Confirm the surge's origin with source-of-traffic data (client IP / user-agent / ASN) at the edge or WAF, and, if unavailable in current telemetry, instrument it — to distinguish an external flood or credential-stuffing campaign from original-client retry behavior.
recommended_actions.rationale: H4's origin sub-hop is inferred, not measured; the metric layer exposes no source breakdown, and this decides whether remediation is external-source blocking versus caller retry mitigation. Same-bucket onset and gateway volume always >= auth volume make caller amplification unlikely but not excluded.

recommended_actions.action: Add auth-service capacity and headroom safeguards: raise the fixed worker pool sizing and re-tune maxReplicas so that normal peak (~400 req/s baseline) plus surge has headroom, and alert on worker-pool utilization and accept-queue depth before saturation.
recommended_actions.rationale: The service hit its provisioned ceiling at ~4x baseline with no deployment or config change to blame; a fixed 64-worker pool and maxReplicas 8 provide no burst headroom, converting a demand spike directly into 503s.

recommended_actions.action: Verify recovery by confirming p99 returns to ~82-97ms, error_rate to ~0.1-0.32%, CPU below ~40%, rate_limited_per_min back to ~1.5-2.3/min, and zero new 'accept queue full' 503 entries; validate the gateway's error_rate and p99 return to ~0.13-0.24% and ~204-217ms.
recommended_actions.rationale: These are the verified pre-onset baselines on both auth-service and api-gateway and give an unambiguous recovery criterion for the same 06:54Z step change.

recommended_actions.action: Add per-endpoint and per-route request/error/latency dimensions to auth-service and api-gateway metrics so surge confinement (e.g. POST /v1/auth/login only vs service-wide) and the consuming rate-limit rule can be measured directly rather than inferred from a 503 log signature.
recommended_actions.rationale: No per-endpoint or per-route dimension exists on either service (request_rate_by_endpoint and requests_by_route returned not_found), which is the root reason login confinement remains an inference and which limit rule consumed ~900/min cannot be identified.

recommended_actions.action: Expose per-downstream-backend attribution on api-gateway (per-route/per-backend request, 5xx and latency) and ensure gateway INFO logs carry routing/upstream labels; raise log verbosity on auth-service back above WARN during incidents.
recommended_actions.rationale: Gateway exposes only service-level metrics and emitted no auth-related or WARN/ERROR log entries in the onset window, and the cfg-2801 INFO->WARN change suppressed per-route request logs, so neither side can attribute the 5xx/latency rise to a named backend directly.

recommended_actions.action: Add telemetry or a timeout/health contract for kyc-provider (has_telemetry=false) and latency/error visibility for redis-cache and user-db (only DB-specific metrics, no request latency), so external-dependency and DB-side contributions to auth-service worker saturation can be ruled in or out during future incidents.
recommended_actions.rationale: kyc-provider is unobservable by construction and user-db exposes no request latency metric; the untestability of H5 and any DB-side contributor is a standing blind spot on the auth-service login path.

data_gaps: No per-endpoint or per-route metric dimension exists on auth-service or api-gateway (request_rate_by_endpoint and requests_by_route queries returned not_found; each exposes only 7 service-level series). Therefore whether the ~4x surge is CONFINED to POST /v1/auth/login or is service-wide cannot be measured, and the login-confinement reading rests solely on the 503 log signature.

No source-of-traffic breakdown (client IP, user-agent, ASN) is exposed, so it cannot be determined whether the surge is organic load, brute-force credential stuffing, or retry from the original client or an upstream caller.
kyc-provider is an external vendor component with has_telemetry=false, so its latency/error rate is unobservable from this platform; the external-dependency hypothesis H5 cannot be tested either way.

user-db exposes only DB-specific metrics (connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min) with no request latency metric, so a DB-side contribution to auth-service worker saturation remains unverified.

redis-cache has no latency or error metric; its health was assessed only via CPU, connections, evictions (all flat). Hit_ratio_pct and memory_pct were not retrieved, so a cache-miss/inference sub-path of the shared-cache hypothesis is unverified, though CPU/connections/evictions were flat.

Change search covered deployments and config only; schema migrations, feature-flag flips outside the config system, and cron/job changes were not enumerated, so a non-deployment, non-config auth-path change cannot be positively excluded.
Metric buckets are 6 minutes (120s for the zoomed comparison), so the true onset is bounded to the 06:48-06:54Z bucket boundary (surge inside 06:48-06:50Z) rather than pinned to an exact second.
api-gateway non-error (INFO) log lines were not retrieved (ERROR and WARN queries were both empty), so the gateway may hold routing/upstream labels at INFO that were not seen.

The login-filtered ERROR query was truncated (104 matches, 20 returned), and cfg-2801 suppressed INFO per-route request logs on auth-service, so no request-path logs exist to reconstruct which endpoints received the excess volume.

Sibling backends (portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) were proven latency-flat but their own HTTP 5xx error rates in the window were not retrieved, so 'no errors on siblings' is not directly evidenced.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Source-of-traffic data showing the ~4x surge originates from upstream callers or the platform's own retrying components (rather than an external source) would move the conclusion from an external inbound flood toward caller-driven retry amplification, changing the mitigation from edge blocking to fixing the amplifying caller.

A measured per-endpoint breakdown showing the ~4x rise is service-wide across all auth-service endpoints rather than concentrated on POST /v1/auth/login would weaken the credential-stuffing reading of the surge (though not the capacity-saturation mechanism).

Evidence of a redis-cache-side degradation or of one of the shared co-tenants (portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) degrading at or before 06:54Z would reopen the shared-cache hypothesis H3, which is currently contradicted by flat cache CPU/connections/evictions and latency-flat co-tenants.

Discovery of an unrecorded auth-path change near onset (a feature-flag flip, schema migration, or job change outside the deployment/config systems) that alters crypto cost or request handling would reopen H2, which is currently excluded by zero auth-service deployments in-window and prior week, no config/flag change near onset, and no bcrypt/timeout/OOM log signature.

Evidence of kyc-provider stalls (or of a synchronous kyc-provider call on the login path with no timeout) would raise H5 from untestable floor to a live mechanism, since that dependency is unobservable from this platform by construction.

Evidence of memory pressure, restarts, or OOM behavior on auth-service would contradict the demand-driven saturation mechanism; these are currently excluded by memory staying at 48-57% and restarts at 0.

Evidence that auth-service inbound request volume exceeded or preceded api-gateway-forwarded volume in any aligned bucket would indicate retry/duplicate amplification at the gateway, contradicting the same-bucket matching-rise finding (F38/F40/F43).

findings.statement: Only ONE deployment occurred across ALL services in the incident window 2026-04-22T00:00Z–08:59Z: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (dep-5803) at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z, summary 'Holdings export', change 'CSV export endpoint', status live, not rolled back. No auth-service deployment appears in this window.
auth-service had ZERO deployments in the week 2026-04-15T00:00Z–2026-04-22T09:00Z, so any bcrypt-style code change would have to predate 2026-04-15.

The only config change on auth-service in the window (and in the prior week) is cfg-2801: log.level INFO→WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot, described as 'Reduce log volume' — a logging change, not an auth-path or bcrypt change.

auth-service's direct dependencies: outbound to user-db (kind 'db', postgres, shared=false), redis-cache (kind 'cache', shared=true), kyc-provider (kind 'external', vendor, has_telemetry=false); inbound edge api-gateway → auth-service (kind 'http'). Its own node is marked shared=false.

redis-cache is the ONE shared component on auth-service's path: it also serves portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service. portfolio-service — the only service deployed in the window (05:50Z) — is therefore coupled to auth-service through this shared cache. user-db, by contrast, is used only by auth-service (no other upstream edges).

The cited precedent exists: HIST-101, 2025-08-14, 'Login latency after auth-service release', symptoms 'login p99 4s','503 on login','high cpu', root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', resolution 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. Its trigger was a deployment; no auth-service deployment has occurred here. HIST-107 (2025-12-09, cold cache storm after redis failover on redis-cache) is the other historical incident touching a component shared with auth-service.

findings.statement: Timeline inference: the two change events in the window bracket the incident onset — auth-service log.level change at 03:40Z (3h26m before the 07:06Z report) and portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z (1h16m before the report). Neither is an auth-service code release, so the 'bcrypt regression after an auth-service release' mechanism cannot be reproduced from change data alone; an infrastructure/shared-cache path (redis-cache, shared with portfolio-service) is not excluded.

auth-service p99 latency was flat at ~82-97 ms through 06:48Z, then jumped to ~3.75s in the 06:54Z bucket (3752.4 ms avg / 4012.81 ms max) — a ~40x step change — and stayed elevated ~3.7-4.0s through the end of the window. Onset bucket: 2026-04-22T06:54:00Z (first sub-normal bucket boundary 06:54, previous normal bucket 06:48).
auth-service error_rate (% HTTP 5xx) was ~0.1-0.32% through 06:48Z, then rose to 11.72% in the 06:54Z bucket and settled ~13.7-14.4% thereafter. Same onset bucket (06:54Z) as the latency jump.

auth-service CPU was ~36-40% through 06:42Z, then climbed in the 06:48Z bucket (avg 56.79, max 96.96) and saturated at ~96-98% from 06:54Z onward for the rest of the window. CPU saturation precedes/coincides with the latency and error onset.

auth-service ERROR logs are exclusively one signature: 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)' — 372 occurrences, first_seen 2026-04-22T06:55:42Z, last 08:58:57Z. There is NO bcrypt-related, timeout, connection-refused, or OOM error signature in auth-service logs. The incident report's bcrypt-regression guess is not supported by the log signatures.

findings.statement: The named dependencies 'session-store' and 'user-profile' do not exist as monitored services; the actual known services are user-db, redis-cache, kafka, api-gateway, ledger-db, etc. A query for user-db latency_p99_ms failed because user-db exposes only DB-specific metrics: connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min — so it has no request latency metric and its health must be judged via those.

Re-querying deployments for ALL services in 2026-04-22T05:00Z–07:30Z (which fully contains the 06:54Z onset) returns exactly one deployment: dep-5803 portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z, 'CSV export endpoint', status live, not rolled back. No deployment lands within ~60 minutes before onset.
A config-change query for ALL services in 2026-04-22T05:00Z–07:30Z returns count 0 — no config or flag change occurred near the 06:54Z onset.

The only config change on any service in the early window is cfg-2801: auth-service log.level INFO→WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot, description 'Reduce log volume' — 3h14m before onset and unrelated to auth-path code or bcrypt cost.

Temporal-distance comparison of the two change events against the 06:54Z onset (T1/T2): portfolio-service dep-5803 (05:50Z, ref tc-017) is 64 min before, auth-service cfg-2801 (03:40Z, ref tc-021) is 194 min before; no change is within the 06:48–06:54Z adjacency. Neither change's payload touches bcrypt/cost factor or auth-service request handling.

The precedent closest in keyword match to this incident (score 4.5) is HIST-101, whose bcrypt cost 10→14 was triggered by release v6.4.0 and resolved by rollback; it is a bad_deployment-category event. Since no auth-service release exists anywhere near this onset, the precedent's trigger mechanism has no counterpart here — symptom similarity alone does not carry over.

findings.statement: Dependency topology: auth-service's only inbound caller is api-gateway, and redis-cache is the sole shared component on its path — it also serves portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service (all have_telemetry:true); auth-service's own outbound edges (user-db, redis-cache) were not re-enumerated this round beyond the shared cache.

Request rate to auth-service was flat at baseline ~382-413 req/s across 06:30Z-06:48Z (avg 394.82 at 06:30Z, 413.26 at 06:36Z, 382.54 at 06:48Z), then SPIKED: 671.71 req/s in the 06:51Z bucket, 1154.93 in 06:54Z, peaking at 1641.69 avg / 1813.74 max in 06:57Z, and holding ~1400-1550 req/s thereafter. The onset of the surge (between the 06:48Z and 06:51Z buckets) precedes/coincides with the 06:54Z latency/error onset, so the rate ROSE rather than stayed flat or fell.

rate_limited_per_min was ~1.5-2.3 req/min throughout 06:30Z-06:51Z (e.g. 1.93 at 06:48Z, 1.46 at 06:51Z), then exploded to 607.72 req/min in the 06:54Z bucket, 852.3 at 06:57Z, and ~885-916 req/min sustained to 07:30Z. This ~400x jump in throttling (min 0.8 -> 949.79) confirms the load was far beyond capacity and being rejected, consistent with an inbound flood/burst rather than a gradual internal slowdown.

memory_pct on auth-service stayed in a normal band ~48-57% across the whole 06:30Z-07:30Z window, including onset (52.23 avg at 06:54Z, 51.05 at 06:57Z, max never above 57.07). Memory pressure/exhaustion is NOT present at onset.

auth-service restarts (metric name 'restarts', cumulative) were 0 across the entire 06:30Z-07:30Z window: every bucket avg 0.0, max 0.0, summary min 0.0 / max 0.0. No restarts occurred, so the incident is not explained by pod crashes/restart loops.

Zooming into the onset with a 480s bucket grid shows the last clean baseline bucket 06:24Z-06:32Z at avg 394.47/403.56 req/s, then the 06:48Z-06:56Z bucket already blended upward to avg 596.44 max 1012.36 — i.e. the surge begins inside the 06:48-06:56 interval, matching the 06:51Z sub-bucket rise and preceding the 06:54Z latency/error jump.

Verdict: inbound request rate SPIKED (~2.9x at 06:54Z: 1154.93 vs ~394 baseline; peak 1641.69 avg / 1813.74 max), it did not stay flat or drop. Combined with rate_limited_per_min exploding to ~900/min while memory (48-57%) and restarts (0) stayed normal, the traffic-surge hypothesis (H4) is supported and the 'flat/lower traffic with internal CPU/queue saturation' form of H1 is contradicted on the inbound-rate dimension.

redis-cache CPU was flat and healthy across 06:00-07:30Z: mean 22.09%, min 20.59%, max 25.59%, with no step change at or before the 06:54Z onset (e.g. 06:50=21.58, 06:55=21.55, 07:00=22.10). The shared cache shows no resource saturation.

redis-cache has no latency or error metric at all — its only available metrics are connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct. So a cache-side latency/error signal must be inferred from connections/evictions/hit-ratio/memory.

redis-cache connected_clients is flat and stable across the window: mean 309.15, range 280.39-336.83, no spike at 06:54Z (06:50=308.03, 06:55=305.63, 07:00=307.43). No surge of blocked/held connections on the shared cache.

redis-cache evictions_per_min is flat and low throughout: mean 2.96, range 0.88-4.9, no rise at 06:54Z (06:50=3.04, 06:55=3.06, 07:00=2.87). No memory-pressure/eviction storm like HIST-107's cold-cache storm.

portfolio-service (the only service deployed in the window, v4.4.0 at 05:50Z) shows NO latency degradation: p99 flat at ~180ms across 06:00-07:30Z (mean 180.62, min 164.72, max 201.36), unchanged through the 06:54Z onset bucket (06:50=183.76, 06:55=178.88, 07:00=180.59). The deployed co-tenant did not degrade.

The other two redis-cache co-tenants also show NO degradation at or before 06:54Z: pricing-engine p99 flat ~60ms (mean 60.06, min 55.26, max 67.23) and market-data-service p99 flat ~40ms (mean 39.95, min 35.67, max 43.75), both unchanged through the onset bucket. All three shared consumers are healthy, so the fault is NOT at the shared cache.

api-gateway exposes only service-level metrics (cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts) — there is NO per-downstream-backend breakdown dimension in the metric API, and api-gateway emitted zero ERROR/WARN log entries in 06:45–07:15Z, so the gateway itself does not attribute its 5xx/latency to a named backend.

api-gateway error_rate was flat ~0.13–0.24% through the 06:51Z bucket, then jumped to 6.23% (max 9.4) in the 06:54Z bucket and plateaued ~8.85–9.53% thereafter — same 06:54Z onset bucket as auth-service, delta ≈ +9.0 pp.

api-gateway latency_p99_ms was ~204–217 ms through the 06:51Z bucket (avg 207.77) and jumped to 3869.46 ms (max 4024.51) in the 06:54Z bucket, staying ~3.76–4.05 s for the rest of the window — a ~18x step change at the same 06:54Z boundary as auth-service's own p99 jump.

The three backends that share redis-cache with auth-service stayed flat across the entire 06:30–07:30Z window, including through the 06:54Z onset: portfolio-service p99 181.65→182.06→183.8 ms (min 164.72, max 195.22), pricing-engine 59.15→58.38→62.76 ms (min 55.94, max 65.16), market-data-service 38.29→39.44→40.34 ms (min 35.67, max 42.56) — no deviation at onset.

api-gateway request_rate rose ahead of/with the error onset: ~1261–1277 req/s through 06:48Z, 2102.78 in the 06:51Z bucket, then 3530→5247 req/s through 07:30Z (a ~4x increase from baseline 1178–1348 req/s). Gateway load and 5xx rise together while downstream siblings stay flat.

Because redis-cache is the only component shared between auth-service and portfolio-service/pricing-engine/market-data-service (per F5/F19), the fact that all three co-consumers show zero latency or load deviation at the 06:54Z onset while api-gateway's entire 5xx/latency jump is confined to the auth-service path indicates the fault is isolated to auth-service, not a shared-gateway or shared-cache/infrastructure fault.

At identical 120s bucket resolution, api-gateway request_rate and auth-service request_rate first rise in the SAME bucket: gateway goes 1227.99 (06:48Z) -> 1500.82 (06:50Z), auth-service goes 386.14 (06:48Z) -> 452.43 (06:50Z). The gateway does NOT begin rising in an earlier bucket.

Rise factors match: api-gateway climbs from baseline 1227.99 (06:48Z) to 3294.15 (06:54Z), 3939.86 (06:56Z), 4790.49 (06:58Z) and peaks 5247.87 at 07:30Z = ~4.3x; auth-service climbs from 386.14 (06:48Z) to 1094.83 (06:54Z), 1350.36 (06:56Z), 1749.75 (06:58Z, max 1813.74) = ~4.5-4.7x — comparable multiplicative factors, not divergent.

Absolute request volume at auth-service never exceeds the volume api-gateway forwarded, in every aligned bucket: 06:50Z gateway 1500.82 vs auth 452.43; 06:54Z gateway 3294.15 vs auth 1094.83; 06:58Z gateway 4790.49 vs auth 1749.75; gateway remains >3x auth throughout. There is no bucket where auth-service inbound > gateway forwarded volume.

api-gateway exposes only service-level metrics — available_metrics = [cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts] — with no per-route or per-downstream-backend (api-gateway->auth-service) request dimension, so request-level attribution of the gateway's rise to a specific route/backend cannot be measured.

A log query on api-gateway filtered to 'auth' over 06:45-07:15Z returned 0 matches (total_matched 0, truncated false), so api-gateway logs provide no per-route/per-auth-service request attribution either.

Verdict EXTERNAL INBOUND FLOOD: the ~4x request increase appears simultaneously at the edge (api-gateway, 06:50Z) and at auth-service by a matching ~4x factor, with auth-service volume consistently a fraction (roughly 1/3) of the gateway's, i.e. no excess at auth-service beyond what the gateway forwarded — inconsistent with retry/duplicate amplification at the gateway, and consistent with genuine inbound load.

auth-service exposes NO per-endpoint or per-route request dimension: its metric API lists available_metrics = [cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts] — all service-level. A direct query for 'request_rate_by_endpoint' was rejected with not_found and the same 7-metric list.

api-gateway likewise has no per-route dimension: its available_metrics = [cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts], and a query for 'requests_by_route' was rejected with not_found. So no route-level split of the gateway's rise is measurable either.

At 120s resolution auth-service request_rate shows a monotonic service-wide climb starting 06:50Z, not an endpoint breakdown: 386.14 (06:48Z) -> 452.43 (06:50Z) -> 742.81 (06:52Z) -> 1094.83 (06:54Z) -> 1749.75 (06:58Z, peak 1813.74), holding ~1412-1540 req/s through 07:30Z. This is the whole-service inbound rate rising ~4x from a ~386-418 baseline, with no lower-level dimension to localize it.

rate_limited_per_min also exploded at the same 06:54Z boundary: 1.21 (06:52Z) -> 451.86 avg / 902.06 max (06:54Z) -> ~870-920 sustained to 07:30Z (min 0.8, max 949.79). The throttling metric carries no limit-rule or route label — only a scalar per-minute count — so which limit rule/route consumed the ~900/min cannot be identified from it.

The only endpoint-level evidence anywhere is in the logs: the 503 rejections are 100% POST /v1/auth/login — a 'login'-filtered ERROR query returned 104 matches, all top_pattern 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning <n> (POST /v<n>/auth/login)', first_seen 06:55:42Z. No other endpoint appears in any rejection signature.

findings.statement: Confidence bound: because the metric layer exposes no per-endpoint/per-route dimension on either auth-service or api-gateway, the surge cannot be measured as CONFINED to login or SERVICE-WIDE. The login-specific credential-stuffing reading rests solely on the 503 signature being exclusively POST /v1/auth/login, which is an inference, not a per-endpoint measurement; a genuine service-wide ~4x inbound rise on all endpoints would be indistinguishable in the available metrics.
